title: How Long Will My Pension Last? Years across Balances
metaDescription: How long will my pension last? See exact depletion timelines across balances, monthly withdrawals, and return rates, plus key tax and lump sum rules.
h1: How Long Will My Pension Last?
cardBlurb: Exact depletion math showing how long a pension lump sum lasts across balances, withdrawal amounts, and return rates, plus tax considerations.
introText:
How long your pension money will last depends on three basic numbers: the starting balance, your monthly withdrawal, and your annual return. A $500,000 balance paying $3,000 a month at a 5% return lasts about 23.8 years, whereas at $2,000 a month the money never runs out at 5% because monthly interest ($2,083) exceeds your withdrawal. At ModernWallet, we evaluate retirement scenarios through clear math on stated assumptions rather than vague guesses, because a shift in monthly spending changes your timeline faster than market fluctuations.

This analysis applies to a pension lump sum or a dedicated retirement balance that you manage and spend down directly. A traditional defined benefit pension that pays a monthly benefit for life does not deplete like a savings balance; if you need to calculate your monthly payout instead, use our [pension calculator](/retirement/pension-calculator/). When you manage a finite pool of capital, your withdrawal-to-balance ratio dictates your total runway.

Taking larger distributions quickly drains principal and reduces future earnings. By understanding the math behind balance depletion, return sensitivity, and tax rules, you can design a spending schedule that protects your financial independence for decades.

sections.heading: Depletion Math and the Monthly Interest Check
sections.body:
Portfolio runway relies on the interplay between your regular monthly distribution and the investment growth generated by your remaining principal. Your money lasts a specific number of months, where the balance is drawn down by a fixed withdrawal at the end of each month and the balance earns the annual return divided by 12 each month. If the monthly interest generated by your starting balance is at least equal to your monthly withdrawal, the balance never runs out.

Consider an interest-only threshold calculation. A $500,000 balance earning a 5% annual return produces about $2,083 each month, calculated as $500,000 multiplied by 0.05 and divided by 12. If you withdraw $2,000 each month, your draw sits below that monthly return, leaving your principal intact. When you increase your monthly draw to $3,000, the portfolio cannot generate enough yield to cover the gap, which forces you to sell principal and starts the clock on total depletion.

These projections depend on fixed baseline conditions. The assumptions for these depletion figures are a 5% annual return, credited monthly, a fixed withdrawal at the end of each month, no inflation adjustment to the withdrawal, no taxes, no account fees, and a return that remains constant across the entire period.

sections.heading: Depletion Timelines across Balances and Monthly Draws
sections.body:
Your starting balance and monthly spending determine how many years your funds can sustain distributions before hitting zero. The calculations below follow our stated baseline method: a 5% annual return credited monthly, fixed end-of-month withdrawals, no taxes, no fees, no inflation adjustments, and an unvarying return rate across all years.

| Starting balance | $2,000/mo | $3,000/mo | $4,000/mo | $5,000/mo |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $250,000 | 14.7 years | 8.5 years | 6.0 years | 4.7 years |
| $500,000 | never runs out | 23.8 years | 14.7 years | 10.8 years |
| $750,000 | never runs out | never runs out | 30.5 years | 19.7 years |
| $1,000,000 | never runs out | never runs out | never runs out | 35.9 years |

Small adjustments to your monthly spending lead to major shifts in portfolio longevity. At a $500,000 balance, raising the withdrawal from $3,000 to $4,000 a month cuts the runway from 23.8 years to 14.7 years, which eliminates about nine years of retirement income for a one-third bigger distribution. When a withdrawal matches or exceeds portfolio yield, depletion accelerates rapidly because every sold asset permanently reduces future interest.

Balance scale matters, but the withdrawal-to-balance ratio matters even more. A $4,000 monthly distribution lasts only 6.0 years on a $250,000 balance, yet it lasts 30.5 years on a $750,000 balance. You can test your personal monthly targets in our [retirement income calculator](/retirement/retirement-income-calculator/) to see where your balance lands.

sections.heading: The Impact of Investment Return on Longevity
sections.body:
Investment returns exert powerful leverage over how long a fixed monthly withdrawal lasts before depletion. To see this sensitivity, examine a $500,000 starting balance supporting a fixed monthly withdrawal of $3,500 across different return levels. The assumptions mirror our standard depletion method: monthly compounding, fixed withdrawals at the end of each month, no taxes, no fees, no inflation adjustments, and a constant annual rate.

| Annual return | Years the money lasts |
|---|---|
| 3% | 14.7 years |
| 5% | 18.1 years |
| 7% | 25.7 years |

Shifting your portfolio return alters your timeline dramatically. Moving the return from 3% to 7% almost doubles the runway, stretching it from 14.7 years to 25.7 years on the exact same $3,500 monthly draw. That extra growth funds an additional 11 years of living expenses without requiring you to deposit another dollar of capital.

Market performance rarely stays constant year over year. While a 7% return extends your runway on paper, volatile markets can cause sharp portfolio dips in early retirement. You can evaluate multi-decade horizons and lower withdrawal hurdles using our [early retirement calculator](/retirement/early-retirement-calculator/) to plan around real-world volatility.

sections.heading: Pension Lump Sum versus a Monthly Pension for Life
sections.body:
A traditional defined benefit pension does not run out of money the way an individual savings balance does. Defined benefit plans provide a guaranteed monthly check for your lifetime, backed by an employer plan or insurance pool, meaning the principal depletion math shown on this page does not apply to that structure. If you hold a defined benefit entitlement, explore our [pension vs annuity](/compare/pension-vs-annuity/) analysis to understand lifetime payment structures.

Taking a pension lump sum shifts all investment management and longevity risk onto your own shoulders. A lump sum gives you complete control over your investments and legacy planning, but you bear the entire burden of managing withdrawals. If your distributions run too high or investment returns lag, you face total exhaustion of the fund.

Comparing options requires weighing steady guaranteed income against investment flexibility. If you prefer building wealth through market assets, our comparison of a [pension vs 401k](/compare/pension-vs-401k/) covers how self-directed retirement balances operate. A lifetime annuity or monthly pension guarantees you cannot outlive your income, whereas a lump sum requires constant discipline to avoid running out of money.

sections.heading: Taxes and Early Withdrawal Rules that Reduce Your Runway
sections.body:
Taxes and IRS distribution penalties can shrink your usable pension balance before you take your first monthly withdrawal. If a pension lump sum is paid directly to you rather than rolled over into an eligible retirement plan, eligible rollover distributions from employer plans generally have 20% federal income tax withheld upfront. Furthermore, the entire distribution is generally treated as taxable income in that tax year, as explained by [IRS Topic 412, lump-sum distributions](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc412).

A direct rollover to an Individual Retirement Account (IRA) generally avoids immediate taxation and mandatory withholding. Setting up a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer preserves your full capital balance so it can generate compounding returns. Make sure to consult your pension plan administrator and a qualified tax professional before requesting any payment, because an improper distribution method triggers immediate taxes.

Age rules impose additional costs on early retirees. Withdrawing funds from a qualified retirement account before reaching age 59 and a half can add a 10% additional tax on early distributions unless a specific exception applies, as detailed by [IRS Topic 558, additional tax on early distributions](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc558). That 10% penalty directly reduces your investable nest egg and shortens your total years of retirement income.

sections.heading: Safe Distribution Strategies to Protect Your Capital
sections.body:
Designing a sustainable withdrawal strategy protects your principal from early exhaustion. The classic 4% guideline comes from the 1998 Trinity Study of historical 30-year periods, which examined sustainable withdrawals across past market cycles. A 30-year or longer retirement sits at the outer edge of what that study modeled; for horizons spanning 35 years or more, research on this site suggests targeting an initial withdrawal rate of 3% to 3.5%.

Structuring your income around variable distributions prevents forced asset sales during market drops. If you manage a smaller balance alongside your pension, reviewing [how long will $150,000 last in retirement](/guides/how-long-will-150k-last-in-retirement/) highlights how quickly modest balances drain under higher spending rates. Incorporating flexible spending rules helps you navigate rough market patches without depleting core savings.

Review your withdrawal rate annually and maintain a short-term cash buffer to absorb living costs during market declines. To build a comprehensive distribution plan across all your investment accounts, explore our guide to [retirement withdrawal strategies](/guides/retirement-withdrawal-strategies/). If you hold traditional tax-deferred accounts, plan ahead for eventual mandatory distributions with our [RMD calculator](/retirement/rmd-calculator/) to avoid unexpected tax hits.

faqs.question: How long will $500,000 last in retirement?
faqs.answer: How long $500,000 lasts depends on your monthly withdrawal rate and investment return. At a 5% annual return, taking $3,000 a month lasts about 23.8 years, taking $4,000 a month lasts 14.7 years, and taking $5,000 a month lasts 10.8 years. If you limit your withdrawal to $2,000 a month at a 5% return, the balance never runs out because the monthly interest of $2,083 exceeds your draw.

faqs.question: What monthly withdrawal makes a pension lump sum last forever?
faqs.answer: A pension lump sum lasts indefinitely when your monthly withdrawal stays at or below the monthly interest earned on the balance. For example, a $500,000 balance earning a 5% annual return produces about $2,083 in monthly interest, meaning a $2,000 monthly withdrawal never touches principal. Whenever your monthly distributions stay lower than your monthly earnings, the fund does not deplete.

faqs.question: Does inflation shorten how long my pension lasts?
faqs.answer: Yes, inflation shortens your actual retirement runway if you increase your monthly withdrawals to keep up with rising prices. The depletion tables shown here assume fixed, unadjusted monthly dollar withdrawals over time. If you raise your withdrawals each year to maintain your purchasing power, your portfolio principal drains noticeably faster than these static models show.

faqs.question: Is a pension lump sum taxable?
faqs.answer: Yes, a pension lump sum is generally treated as taxable income in the year it is distributed if paid directly to you. In that scenario, employer plans generally withhold 20% for federal income taxes automatically. You can generally avoid immediate taxation and withholding by executing a direct rollover into an Individual Retirement Account (IRA).

faqs.question: Should I take the lump sum or the monthly pension?
faqs.answer: Choosing between a lump sum and a monthly pension depends on whether you prefer lifetime income guarantees or investment control. A monthly pension guarantees predictable checks for life, eliminating the danger of running out of money. A lump sum gives you control over investments and inheritance options, but you bear the entire risk of managing withdrawals and portfolio depletion.
